      38                 :             : /// \brief Static class which allows creating a singleton in a thread safe manner.
      39                 :             : ///
      40                 :             : /// The potential issues associated with creating singletons in a multithreaded context is described in Ticket-247205.
      41                 :             : /// The root cause appears to be a compiler bug in gcc (which is not present in clang):
      42                 :             : ///   https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=99613/
      43                 :             : ///
      44                 :             : /// The issue is summarised here:
      45                 :             : ///
      46                 :             : /// Constructing static objects:
      47                 :             : ///   The standard states that, in the context of initializing a static variable, "If control enters the declaration
      48                 :             : ///   concurrently while the variable is being initialized, the concurrent execution shall wait for completion of the
      49                 :             : ///   initialization." (Ref: https://eel.is/c++draft/stmt.dcl#3).
      50                 :             : ///
      51                 :             : /// Destruction sequence of static objects:
      52                 :             : ///   The standard guarantees (paraphrased to omit the lawyer language) that if a static object is created before
      53                 :             : ///   another static object, then the second object will be destroyed before the first. (Ref:
      54                 :             : ///   https://eel.is/c++draft/basic.start.term#4)
      55                 :             : ///
      56                 :             : /// Based on these two points, we consider the following case:
      57                 :             : ///   Thread A tries to initialize static object X and then static object Y.
      58                 :             : ///   Thread B tries to initialize static object X.
      59                 :             : ///
      60                 :             : /// There are 3 possible sequences of interest:
      61                 :             : ///  1. Thread A initializes X, Thread A initializes Y, Thread B reads X.
      62                 :             : ///  2. Thread A initializes X, Thread B tries to initialize X but it's already being initialized by thread A so it
      63                 :             : ///  waits for thread A to finish, Thread A initializes Y.
      64                 :             : ///  3. Thread B initializes X, Thread A tries to initialize X but it's already being initialized by thread B so it
      65                 :             : ///  waits for thread B to finish, Thread A initializes Y.
      66                 :             : ///
      67                 :             : /// In all these cases, from the perspective of both threads, X was initialized before Y and therefore Y should be
      68                 :             : /// destroyed before X. However, in practice, we see that sometimes although both threads see that X was initialized
      69                 :             : /// before Y, X is still destroyed before Y. This can lead to a crash if Y relies on X in its destruction sequence.
      70                 :             : ///
      71                 :             : /// Workaround:
      72                 :             : ///
      73                 :             : /// Atomic operations tagged memory_order_seq_cst (default) order memory such that everything that happened-before a
      74                 :             : /// store in one thread becomes a visible side effect in the thread that did a load. (Ref:
      75                 :             : /// https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/atomic/memory_order.html) This means that memory / operations cannot be reordered
      76                 :             : /// around the atomic load. I.e. if X is initialized before the atomic load and Y is constructed after the atomic
      77                 :             : /// load, then the creation order of these two cannot be reordered.
      78                 :             : ///
      79                 :             : /// We therefore store an atomic pointer to the static object which is loaded by any thread which wants to access the
      80                 :             : /// static object, creating a compiler barrier / fence which prevents reordering.
